Issue summary: A QUIC server that rejects a stream opened by the peer may retain that stream's state for the lifetime of the connection if the peer resets the stream before the rejection is signalled, even though the peer's stream credit is returned.  Impact summary: A remote client that completes a QUIC handshake can repeatedly open and reset streams, causing server memory to grow without bound until the process runs out of memory and every connection on it is lost. This is a Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-401: Missing Release of Memory after Effective Lifetime  Description: QUIC servers track each stream the peer opens. When the incoming stream policy rejects a stream, OpenSSL schedules a STOP_SENDING frame, marks the stream deleted and returns the peer's stream credit. A deleted stream is collected only once its receive part is fully drained, which for a rejected stream means the STOP_SENDING has been acknowledged. If the peer sends RESET_STREAM first, the reset cancels the pending STOP_SENDING, so it is never sent or acknowledged and the stream is never collected.  The default configuration reaches this path. Once a connection has a default stream, meaning the application has read from or written to the connection as the tutorial server does, the effective incoming stream policy rejects streams the application does not accept. Applications that set the REJECT policy explicitly are affected too.  Each retained stream costs about 300 bytes, and the peer's stream credit window paces how quickly they accumulate. A client that keeps the connection open and keeps opening and resetting streams grows server memory without bound. The severity is Low because growth is slow, needs a long-lived connection, and causes no memory corruption or disclosure.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

Issue summary: A server configured with the Suite B certificate flag through SSL_CTX_set_cert_flags() and with TLS 1.3 enabled may read past the end of a fixed group list when it processes a ClientHello whose supported_groups and key_share contain no Suite B group.  Impact summary: A remote client can send a ClientHello that makes the server read past the end of a static array. The values read are never returned to the client, so no memory is disclosed; on builds with sanitizers or hardened allocators the read may crash the process, causing Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read  Description: When the Suite B certificate flag is set, OpenSSL restricts the accepted groups to P-256 and P-384 by substituting a fixed two-element list for the configured group list. The tuple machinery used for key-share selection was not updated for this substitution: tls1_get_group_tuples() still returns the configured tuples, which by default describe eight groups. The server-side walk in tls_parse_ctos_key_share() then advances through the two-element list using those tuple counts without checking the cumulative offset against the number of groups present.  Only applications that call SSL_CTX_set_cert_flags() with SSL_CERT_FLAG_SUITEB_128_LOS and leave TLS 1.3 enabled are affected. The openssl s_server -suiteB_128 option sets an X.509 verification parameter instead, so the stock command line server is not vulnerable. Default configurations do not reach this code.  A client that offers only groups outside the Suite B set, such as X25519, forces every tuple to be walked and the read to run past the array. The bytes read are compared against client group IDs and never sent back, so no memory is disclosed. On builds with address sanitizers or hardened allocators the read can abort the process; in ordinary release builds it reads a few bytes of adjacent constant data.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

They state that the worst outcome this issue can cause is a crash of diff and that it cannot be used to escalate privileges.

Issue summary: QUIC, when performing automated peer detection, may allow uninitialized stack data to leak into the received address which is then used as the destination for outgoing packets.  Impact summary: Applications using QUIC's automated peer detection mechanism may receive an invalid address, leading to connection loss and disclosure of uninitialized stack data to an attacker observing the outgoing network traffic.  CWE: CWE-457 (Use of Uninitialized Variable)  Description: The OpenSSL QUIC stack contains a feature in which, when using an already connected socket, it will auto-detect the peer address during the SSL handshake.  This feature uses the getpeername() function, passing a buffer of sufficient length to hold any supported address family, but passes a buffer length that is only sized such that larger addresses, such as IPv6, cannot be retrieved. The getpeername() function however, still returns the full address length, which is accepted as the valid input buffer length, leading to the address buffer containing uninitialized stack data instead of the actual peer address. The invalid peer address is then used as destination for the outgoing packets which leads to a connectivity breakage and a leakage of the uninitialized stack data to passive network observers.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules in 4.0, 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, and 3.0 are not affected by this CVE as the affected protocol is not implemented in the FIPS module.

Issue summary: The AES-GCM-SIV implementation treats a zero-length Additional Authenticated Data (AAD) update as a reset of all the AAD supplied so far, instead of leaving the AAD unchanged. An application that supplies its AAD in several fragments, one of which is empty, therefore produces or verifies messages whose authentication tag does not cover the AAD supplied before the empty fragment.  Impact summary: Data an application intended to authenticate alongside a message is silently left unauthenticated. An attacker can forge the AAD of such a message.  CWE: CWE-325: Missing Cryptographic Step  Description: An application passing AAD in multiple chunks of which some have zero length will have the previous AAD chunks effectively unauthenticated. Also, on context re-initialisation, the AAD was not reset, which meant that any AAD accumulated from the previous context usage were also included in the AAD of the new message.  The fix makes a zero-length AAD update a no-op and clears any accumulated AAD whenever the context is re-initialised with a key or a nonce. A re-initialisation that only changes parameters keeps the AAD.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules are not affected, as AES-GCM-SIV is not a FIPS approved algorithm and is implemented only in the default provider, outside the OpenSSL FIPS module boundary.

Issue summary: Setting an AES-GCM-SIV IV shorter than the expected nonce length via EVP_CipherInit_ex() may trigger a heap out-of-bounds read. Supplying a longer IV is silently truncated instead of rejected.  Impact summary: An application passing a caller-supplied IV of the wrong length may crash or read beyond its buffer. Because trailing IV bytes are ignored, an attacker who knows one message and tag may forge messages under a different IV.  CWE: CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read  Description: AES-GCM-SIV copies the caller-supplied IV or nonce into its internal state using a copy whose length is taken from the expected nonce size rather than from the length the caller actually provided. When the caller passes a shorter IV, the copy reads past the end of the caller's buffer; AddressSanitizer confirms a heap out-of-bounds read reached through EVP_CipherInit_ex() into ossl_aes_gcm_siv_init(). When the caller passes a longer IV, the implementation silently discards the trailing bytes instead of rejecting the length.  The truncation breaks the binding between the IV and the computed authentication tag. An attacker who has observed a message and its tag under one IV can produce a message and tag that verify under a different IV whose first bytes match, since the surplus bytes never influence the computation. help.text:
### Summary

On Windows, attacker-controlled content in a wheel's
`.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt` can cause setuptools' legacy wheel
installation path to create an `__init__.py` outside the requested
`destination_eggdir`.

The attacker can influence the destination path, but not the contents of
the created file.

### Details

Tested setuptools commit:

`6ead555c5fb29bc57fe6105b1bffc163f56fd558`

Relevant source:

`setuptools/wheel.py`

SHA-256:

`359b7e0d5dd8c3135653abe08a8ed5dc0352eadfd7df22cb5e2b5303b7c3cafd`

The relevant call path is:

`Wheel(wheel_path).install_as_egg(destination)`
→ `_install_as_egg`
→ `_convert_metadata`
→ `_fix_namespace_packages`

A wheel can provide attacker-controlled content in:

`<distribution>.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`

The namespace value is eventually used approximately as:

```python
mod_dir = os.path.join(destination_eggdir, *mod.split('.'))
mod_init = os.path.join(mod_dir, '__init__.py')

If mod is a Windows drive-qualified absolute path containing no dots,
mod.split('.') preserves it as a single component.
On Windows, os.path.join(destination_eggdir, absolute_component) discards
the original base directory and resolves to the attacker-supplied absolute
path.
The existing wheel filename and ZIP traversal checks do not validate this
metadata value before it is subsequently interpreted as a filesystem path.

```markdown
### PoC

The reproduction was performed entirely inside a disposable temporary
directory.

Layout:

```text
sandbox/
    destination/
    outside/
    input/
    canary.txt
```

A synthetic wheel was created containing:

`demo_pkg-1.0.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`

whose content was the absolute path of:

`sandbox\outside`

The real acquired setuptools implementation was then invoked:

```python
setuptools.wheel.Wheel(synthetic_wheel).install_as_egg(
    sandbox_destination
)
```

The operation completed without exception.

Expected metadata was created under:

`sandbox\destination\EGG-INFO`

but setuptools also created:

`sandbox\outside\__init__.py`

The file did not exist before execution.

Its contents were:

```python
__import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(__name__)
```

The unrelated canary remained byte-identical.

The sandbox was deleted after recording the evidence.
```


### Impact

A crafted wheel can cause setuptools to create a fixed-content
`__init__.py` outside the intended installation directory at a
filesystem path influenced by the wheel, with the permissions of the
process performing the installation.

The demonstrated reproduction required the target parent directory to
already exist.

The glob functions in the GNU C Library versions 2.44 and earlier may free the same heap block twice when a memory allocation fails while glob prepends the directory name to the names it matched.  The names already rewritten are freed, but their pointers stay in the result vector, and the error path frees them again with globfree.  The allocation must fail after at least one name has been rewritten, so the issue can only be reached when the process is already close to its memory limit, for example under an address space limit (RLIMIT_AS) or on a 32-bit system.  The attacker needs control to make the result large enough to make the program or service run out of memory, either by controlling the glob pattern and having knowledge of the filesystem layout or through other means.  This issue affects all architectures and ABIs supported by the GNU C Library.

GNU Tar through 1.35 allows file overwrite via directory traversal in crafted TAR archives, with a certain two-step process. First, the victim must extract an archive that contains a ../ symlink to a critical directory. Second, the victim must extract an archive that contains a critical file, specified via a relative pathname that begins with the symlink name and ends with that critical file's name. Here, the extraction follows the symlink and overwrites the critical file. This bypasses the protection mechanism of "Member name contains '..'" that would occur for a single TAR archive that attempted to specify the critical file via a ../ approach. For example, the first archive can contain "x -> ../../../../../home/victim/.ssh" and the second archive can contain x/authorized_keys. This can affect server applications that automatically extract any number of user-supplied TAR archives, and were relying on the blocking of traversal. This can also affect software installation processes in which "tar xf" is run more than once (e.g., when installing a package can automatically install two dependencies that are set up as untrusted tarballs instead of official packages).

The nscd service in the GNU C Library 2.3.4 onwards may crash due to a  stack overflow when a malicious DNS server returns too large a response  for a DNS query, resulting in degraded DNS resolution for the system.    Exploitation of this bug needs a system that has nscd enabled and using  an untrusted DNS server for name resolution, with the compromised DNS  server being capable of processing records large enough to result in a  stack overflow in an nscd thread stack.  During experimentation, bind 9  was unable to handle large records, but that could change in future or  with a different name server.  In typical installations, nscd is  executed in an isolated context as its own user without a shell, due to  which any compromise of that service is isolated.    There is a remote possibility of nscd cache corruption if an attacker  manages to get the stack pointer into a desired point in the heap,  potentially resulting in other caches in nscd being overwritten with  corrupt data through the stack overflow, until the buggy code path  eventually results in a crash.    Finally, a crash in nscd may result in performance degradation when  resolving names, but it does not result in a denial of service.

Initializing the DNS stub resolver from an /etc/resolv.conf file, or a LOCALDOMAIN environment variable, whose search list contains a domain of roughly 200 characters or more in the GNU C Library version 2.26 to 2.44 results in an assertion failure which aborts the process.  The resolver truncates the search list when copying it into the fixed-size _res.defdname buffer, then asserts that the copy is consistent with the full configuration.  The consistency check compared against the wrong size and did not handle a first entry that does not fit, so a correctly truncated list failed the assertion.  Any process that resolves names through the library is affected, including long-running processes that reload /etc/resolv.conf on the next query after it changes.  Search domains are commonly written to /etc/resolv.conf from data received over DHCP or from a VPN server, so an attacker on the local network may be able to trigger this without privileges on the target system, subject to validation by the network configuration software.

Issue summary: Receiving crafted out-of-sequence DTLS handshake fragments may cause OpenSSL to allocate a full message-length reassembly buffer for each buffered message, so a small amount of wire data consumes a large amount of memory.  Impact summary: A remote attacker can send a few small crafted DTLS handshake fragments to make a DTLS server or client allocate well over a megabyte of memory per connection, which may lead to memory exhaustion and Denial of Service if many connections are made.  CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling  Description: DTLS handshake messages can arrive out of order and fragmented, so OpenSSL buffers fragments of up to ten out-of-sequence messages until reassembly is possible. When the first fragment of a new message arrives, OpenSSL allocates a buffer sized to the full message length declared in the fragment header, plus a reassembly bitmap, instead of storing only the bytes actually received. The declared length is capped by the maximum certificate list size, 128KB by default, and that cap applies to every handshake message type rather than only to Certificate messages.  Only DTLS endpoints reach this code. TLS, QUIC and applications that do not use DTLS are unaffected. An attacker sends fragments that declare a large message length but carry almost no data, using up to ten distinct message sequence numbers.  A single connection can then hold roughly 1.4MB of buffers from about 156 bytes on the wire. Because the number of buffered messages is capped, memory exhaustion requires many connections or many peers, which is why the severity is Low.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

Calling tdelete on a sufficiently deep tree in the GNU C Library version 2.1 to 2.44 may write one pointer past the end of an alloca-allocated array on the stack, which may crash the application.  The tdelete implementation keeps an explicit stack of parent nodes for rebalancing, which is grown as needed while descending the tree.  Two rebalancing branches push an additional entry without checking the capacity, and write past the array when the stack is exactly full. Triggering this requires a node at a depth of exactly 40 (or 40 plus a multiple of 20), which implies a tree with at least a million nodes, so an attacker must drive a large number of insertions and deletions through an application that uses tsearch and tdelete.  The written value is a pointer into a tree node and is not directly attacker controlled.  No affected application in common distributions has been identified.

Converting crafted CP949 input to UTF-8 character encoding and ignoring invalid characters, in the GNU C Library version 2.1 or later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.  When the CP949 decoder encounters an invalid input byte sequence like '\xa2\xe8' it ends up advancing the pointer tracking the read buffer position twice. To exploit this, the target iconv function needs to set //IGNORE on the destination of the conversion and the input and encoding needs to be attacker controlled.

Converting crafted input from UCS-4 to IBM1390 or IBM1399 character encoding, in the GNU C Library version 2.3.3 and later may result in the converter reading past the end of the input buffer, causing the calling application to crash.  When converting from UCS-4, these encoders may encounter a combining base such as U+00E6 and jump ahead by 4 bytes to check the next UCS-4 code point.  The check for end of buffer however does not account for this, which may result in a buffer overread if the following code point has less than 4 bytes remaining.  Exploitation of this bug not only requires attacker control of input and encoding, but also strict control over layout of the input in memory.

Converting crafted SHIFT_JISX0213 input to UCS-4 or the internal wide character encoding, for example with iconv, in the GNU C Library version 2.3 to 2.44 may result in the converter making no progress, causing the calling application to hang.  Some SHIFT_JISX0213 sequences decode to two code points.  If the output buffer has room for only the first one, the converter stores the second in the conversion state and returns E2BIG, but it never clears that pending character after emitting it on the next call.  The converter then keeps emitting the pending character without consuming further input, so an application that retries the conversion loops forever. The input must be attacker controlled and the application must convert it with an output buffer small enough to split the two code points. Only the SHIFT_JISX0213 character set is affected, which is not commonly used.  The related defect in the EUC_JISX0213 converter is tracked separately as CVE-2026-80489.

shortDescription.text: CVE-2026-59890: Improper Handling of Unicode Encoding

help.text:
## Summary

When building a source distribution (`python -m build --sdist` / `setup.py sdist`), setuptools' `FileList` applies `MANIFEST.in` directives (`exclude`, `global-exclude`, `recursive-exclude`, `prune`) by matching a compiled glob against on-disk file names **byte-for-byte, with no Unicode normalization**. On normalization-preserving filesystems (notably macOS APFS and HFS+), a file written in NFD and a `MANIFEST.in` rule written in NFC refer to the same file but are byte-distinct, so the exclusion silently fails to match. A file the maintainer intended to exclude is then packed into the `.tar.gz` and, if published, uploaded to the public, immutable PyPI index.

## Details

File names in `FileList.files` come from `os.walk` (`setuptools/_distutils/filelist.py`, `_find_all_simple`), so on APFS a file written NFD is offered to the matcher in NFD, while the `MANIFEST.in` pattern carries the author's editor form (typically NFC). The matching path performs no canonicalization:

```python
# setuptools/command/egg_info.py  (FileList.global_exclude)
def global_exclude(self, pattern):
    match = translate_pattern(os.path.join('**', pattern))   # fnmatch.translate -> regex, no NFC/NFD
    return self._remove_files(match.match)                   # byte-level regex over raw os.walk names
```

A rule written NFC (`café` = `63 61 66 c3 a9`) does not match an on-disk name written NFD (`café` = `63 61 66 65 cc 81`), even though the filesystem treats the two as one file.

A `unicodedata.normalize('NFD', ...)` helper exists in `setuptools/unicode_utils.py` (`decompose()`), but it is **never called in the manifest matching path**, so neither the pattern nor the walked path is normalized before matching. The only normalization in this area, `EggInfoCommand._manifest_normalize`, uses `filesys_decode` (bytes→str decode only, no NFC/NFD) and runs when writing `SOURCES.txt`, after matching has already occurred.

## Impact

`MANIFEST.in` exclusions are the documented mechanism maintainers use to keep secrets, local configs, and private fixtures out of the published sdist. A non-ASCII excluded file may be published to the public, immutable PyPI index despite the rule — an irreversible disclosure with no visual cue (NFC and NFD forms render identically). Exposure is filesystem-dependent and most relevant on macOS APFS/HFS+, where many maintainers build and publish. Pure-ASCII rules are unaffected.

## Proof of concept

With a project containing `MANIFEST.in`:

```
global-include *.txt *.json
global-exclude secret_café.txt    # rule saved NFC
```

and an on-disk file `secret_café.txt` written in NFD, `python -m build --sdist` packs the secret file into the resulting `.tar.gz`, while an ASCII control file excluded by the same directive is correctly dropped — isolating the bypass to the NFC-pattern vs. NFD-name mismatch. Reproduced on macOS APFS with setuptools 82.0.1.

## Remediation

Normalize both the walked path and each `MANIFEST.in` pattern to a single canonical form before matching, in both `setuptools/command/egg_info.py` (`FileList`) and the vendored `setuptools/_distutils/filelist.py`. For an exclusion list, err toward excluding more, and document that `MANIFEST.in` matching is normalization-insensitive on macOS.

## Credit

Reported by Tomas Illuminati. Coordinated via CERT/CC VINCE VU#604762.

On normalization-preserving filesystems (notably macOS APFS and HFS+), a file written in NFD and a `MANIFEST.in` rule written in NFC refer to the same file but are byte-distinct, so the exclusion silently fails to match. A file the maintainer intended to exclude is then packed into the `.tar.gz` and, if published, uploaded to the public, immutable PyPI index.

## Details

File names in `FileList.files` come from `os.walk` (`setuptools/_distutils/filelist.py`, `_find_all_simple`), so on APFS a file written NFD is offered to the matcher in NFD, while the `MANIFEST.in` pattern carries the author's editor form (typically NFC). The matching path performs no canonicalization:

```python
# setuptools/command/egg_info.py  (FileList.global_exclude)
def global_exclude(self, pattern):
    match = translate_pattern(os.path.join('**', pattern))   # fnmatch.translate -> regex, no NFC/NFD
    return self._remove_files(match.match)                   # byte-level regex over raw os.walk names
```

A rule written NFC (`café` = `63 61 66 c3 a9`) does not match an on-disk name written NFD (`café` = `63 61 66 65 cc 81`), even though the filesystem treats the two as one file.

A `unicodedata.normalize('NFD', ...)` helper exists in `setuptools/unicode_utils.py` (`decompose()`), but it is **never called in the manifest matching path**, so neither the pattern nor the walked path is normalized before matching. The only normalization in this area, `EggInfoCommand._manifest_normalize`, uses `filesys_decode` (bytes→str decode only, no NFC/NFD) and runs when writing `SOURCES.txt`, after matching has already occurred.

## Impact

`MANIFEST.in` exclusions are the documented mechanism maintainers use to keep secrets, local configs, and private fixtures out of the published sdist. A non-ASCII excluded file may be published to the public, immutable PyPI index despite the rule — an irreversible disclosure with no visual cue (NFC and NFD forms render identically). Exposure is filesystem-dependent and most relevant on macOS APFS/HFS+, where many maintainers build and publish. Pure-ASCII rules are unaffected.

## Proof of concept

With a project containing `MANIFEST.in`:

```
global-include *.txt *.json
global-exclude secret_café.txt    # rule saved NFC
```

and an on-disk file `secret_café.txt` written in NFD, `python -m build --sdist` packs the secret file into the resulting `.tar.gz`, while an ASCII control file excluded by the same directive is correctly dropped — isolating the bypass to the NFC-pattern vs. NFD-name mismatch. Reproduced on macOS APFS with setuptools 82.0.1.

## Remediation

Normalize both the walked path and each `MANIFEST.in` pattern to a single canonical form before matching, in both `setuptools/command/egg_info.py` (`FileList`) and the vendored `setuptools/_distutils/filelist.py`. For an exclusion list, err toward excluding more, and document that `MANIFEST.in` matching is normalization-insensitive on macOS.

A time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition in the dynamic loader (ld.so) of the GNU C Library (glibc) versions 2.14 through 2.44 allows a local attacker to escalate privileges. When expanding $ORIGIN in DT_RPATH for setuid/setgid (AT_SECURE) programs, glibc validates the lexically normalized search path against the trusted directories but then opens the raw, un-normalized path. On systems where the Linux fs.protected_hardlinks sysctl is disabled, a local attacker who hard-links such a program into an attacker-controlled directory and wins a race to replace an intermediate path component with a symbolic link can direct the loader outside the trusted directory, causing it to load an attacker-controlled shared object and execute arbitrary code with the elevated privileges of the program.  Exploitation requires an installed setuid or setgid binary whose DT_RPATH uses $ORIGIN followed by ".." traversal that normalizes into a trusted directory, and the ability to hard-link that binary and win the race by swapping a path component for a symbolic link. Major Linux-based OS distributions ship with fs.protected_hardlinks enabled by default and mitigate the vulnerability.

When expanding paths that begin with a tilde (~) followed by a username, the internal parse_tilde function extracts the username to determine the user's home directory.  The implementation allocates memory for this username directly on the stack using the strndupa macro. Because the size of this allocation was determined by the length of the user-supplied input without any bounds checks, passing an excessively long username e.g. thousands of characters, forces the thread to exhaust its stack space. Thus if an application passes untrusted, attacker-controlled input to the wordexp function, an attacker can trigger a stack clash.

Issue summary: Encrypting a CMS message to an EC certificate whose group order is 1 may cause CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() to loop indefinitely.  Impact summary: An attacker able to supply the recipient certificate to an application performing CMS encryption can cause that application to loop indefinitely, consuming CPU and resulting in Denial of Service.  CWE: CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')  Description: CMS_encrypt() and CMS_encrypt_ex() encrypt a message to one or more recipient certificates and, for an EC recipient, generate an ephemeral key in the recipient's group. If the certificate declares a group order of 1, random scalar generation can only produce zero. The key generation routine then retries without limit while waiting for a nonzero private scalar, so the call never returns.  The OpenSSL TLS and QUIC implementations do not use this path. An application is exposed only if it calls CMS_encrypt() or CMS_encrypt_ex() with a recipient certificate whose EC parameters are attacker-controlled. Certificates with normal EC group orders do not trigger the loop.  OpenSSL 4.0 and later reject unknown explicit EC groups in default builds. These versions are affected only when configured with the enable-ec_explicit_curves option.  The result is a hang that consumes a CPU core until the process is interrupted, a Denial of Service. The severity is Low because the attacker must supply the recipient certificate and the application must choose to encrypt to it; ordinary CMS encryption to trusted recipients is unaffected.  The fix makes EC key generation fail when the group has no valid nonzero private scalar, instead of retrying indefinitely.  FIPS impact: no The FIPS modules in 4.1, 4.0, 3.5 and 3.0 are not affected. The FIPS provider does not support arbitrary explicit EC domain parameters, so an order-1 group is rejected during key import before the vulnerable key generation path is reached.

### Summary 
A path traversal vulnerability in `PackageIndex` was fixed in setuptools version 78.1.1

### Details
```
    def _download_url(self, url, tmpdir):
        # Determine download filename
        #
        name, _fragment = egg_info_for_url(url)
        if name:
            while '..' in name:
                name = name.replace('..', '.').replace('\\', '_')
        else:
            name = "__downloaded__"  # default if URL has no path contents

        if name.endswith('.[egg.zip](http://egg.zip/)'):
            name = name[:-4]  # strip the extra .zip before download

 -->       filename = os.path.join(tmpdir, name)
```

Here: https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/blob/6ead555c5fb29bc57fe6105b1bffc163f56fd558/setuptools/package_index.py#L810C1-L825C88

`os.path.join()` discards the first argument `tmpdir` if the second begins with a slash or drive letter.
`name` is derived from a URL without sufficient sanitization. While there is some attempt to sanitize by replacing instances of '..' with '.', it is insufficient.

### Risk Assessment
As easy_install and package_index are deprecated, the exploitation surface is reduced.
However, it seems this could be exploited in a similar fashion like https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r9hx-vwmv-q579, and as described by POC 4 in https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cx63-2mw6-8hw5 report: via malicious URLs present on the pages of a package index.

### Impact
An attacker would be allowed to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem with the permissions of the process running the Python code, which could escalate to RCE depending on the context.

Issue summary: When an application passes a stack to PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() to add entries to, and reading fails, OpenSSL frees every entry in the stack, both the old ones and any new ones, but leaves them in the stack.  Impact summary: An application that passes an existing stack to PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() and keeps using it after a failed read may use memory that was already freed. This can cause a crash or, in principle, memory corruption. Malformed PEM data can make the read fail, but only applications that pass an existing stack are affected, and OpenSSL itself does not do this.  CWE: CWE-416: Use After Free  Description: PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio_ex() reads certificates, CRLs and private keys from PEM data and adds them to a stack of X509_INFO structures. If the application passes a stack that is not NULL, the function adds the new entries to it and must leave the entries that are already there unchanged.  If reading fails, the function frees every entry in the stack. This includes the entries that were there before the call, and the entries added by the call. It does not remove these entries from the stack, so the stack keeps pointers to freed memory. The failure can happen at any point, even before any entry was added. A PEM item with invalid content is enough.  This also happens if the stack was empty: entries added before the failure are freed but stay in the stack.  An application that then reads or frees the stack will use memory that was already freed. This can crash the application or, in principle, corrupt memory.  Only applications that pass a stack that is not NULL are affected. OpenSSL itself never does this. Its own callers, including the code that TLS uses to load CA certificates, always pass NULL. When the stack is NULL, the function frees only the entries that it created itself, which is safe. We expect that very few applications pass an existing stack. An attacker can make the read fail with malformed PEM data, but cannot make an application pass an existing stack.  The same problem affects PEM_X509_INFO_read_bio(), PEM_X509_INFO_read() and PEM_X509_INFO_read_ex(), which use the same code. OpenSSL 1.1.1 and 1.0.2 have only the first two of these functions.  FIPS impact: no The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

help.text:
zlib 1.2.11 through 1.3.2 contains a heap buffer overflow: after an underlying write() fails, gz_write() returns without resetting strm.next_in, leaving it pointed at the caller's buffer. A later gz* write call then derives a position from the stale pointer and writes past a heap allocation; any write() failure reaches it, including EPIPE on a blocking descriptor, and in versions before 1.3.1.2 the failed write must be followed by a gzclearerr() call.
